query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating high-throughput laser‐melting drop calorimetry with rapid differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and real‐time synchrotron X‐ray imaging, calibrated against CALPHAD predictions, can accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid‐phase thermodynamic properties across a wide range of high‐entropy alloy compositions.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogenized, single-phase high-entropy alloy samples (e.g., well-mixed BCC or FCC solid solutions produced by arc melting or additive manufacturing) with minimal compositional segregation.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloys to controlled laser-induced melting followed by rapid cooling in a high-throughput DSC setup while simultaneously capturing phase evolution and density changes via synchrotron X-ray imaging, then calibrate these measurements with CALPHAD computations.
generation.conditions: Measurements performed under inert (e.g., argon) atmosphere with temperature control from room temperature up to above the expected liquidus (e.g., up to ~3000°C for refractory systems); approach applicable to alloys with homogeneous microstructures.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniform single-phase microstructure (BCC/FCC) minimizes local segregation and defects, ensuring that melting occurs uniformly, which promotes reliable measurement of latent heat and volume changes.
generation.mechanism: The DSC records the heat flow associated with melting while the laser-drop calorimetry ensures rapid, localized melting; high-speed X-ray imaging tracks volume expansion/contraction. Together with CALPHAD-derived thermodynamic constraints, these data allow extraction of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and density changes with high accuracy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Melting temperatures, latent heat, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting can be determined with uncertainties on the order of ±5–10%, showing systematic trends across different HEA compositions that align with CALPHAD predictions.
generation.baseline: Traditional DSC measurements on conventional binary or ternary alloys with well-established thermodynamic data.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to perform well for HEAs that are compositionally homogeneous and have melting points within the accessible range of the experimental setup; alloys exhibiting significant phase separation, high volatility, or non-equilibrium microstructures may lie outside its effective range.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative performance may be affected by rapid convection in the molten state and minor microstructural inhomogeneities; hence, discrepancies greater than ~15% compared to CALPHAD predictions would indicate limitations of the method.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of homogenized high-entropy alloy samples and subject them to the integrated DSC/laser-drop calorimetry and synchrotron X-ray imaging protocol. Independently measure the melting temperature, latent heat, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting. Compare these experimental results to CALPHAD-predicted values and to standard DSC measurements on conventional alloys. Additionally, intentionally introduce controlled microstructural inhomogeneity in select samples to assess the method’s sensitivity.
measurements: Heat flow curves from DSC during melting
Time-resolved X-ray diffraction data tracking phase change
X-ray imaging data capturing volume change
CALPHAD-predicted thermodynamic parameters for the same compositions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated method consistently yields melting temperatures, enthalpy, entropy, or volume change measurements deviating by more than 15% from both CALPHAD predictions and standard DSC benchmarks, or if slight microstructural inhomogeneities lead to uncontrolled variation in the measured values, then the proposed approach would be refuted.

System: (W 1.5 Ni 2.25 Fe) 95 Ta 5 (at.%) refractory high-entropy alloy with a dual-phase bcc/fcc structure. Processing: Arc melting followed by homogenization at 1200 °C for 5 h, hot rolling at 1200 °C (80% reduction), cold rolling at 25 °C (75% reduction), annealing at 900 °C for 5 min, and aging at 650 °C for 20 h followed by water quenching. Question: How does the addition of Cr to the HfMoTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy affect its phase composition, microstructure, and room-temperature mechanical properties, specifically regarding the synergy between strength and ductility?. System: HfMoTaTiZr (30.0 at% Hf, 16.1 at% Mo, 30.4 at% Ta, 8.1 at% Ti, 15.4 at% Zr) and HfMoTaTiZrCr0.5 (28.8 at% Hf, 15.5 at% Mo, 29.1 at% Ta, 7.7 at% Ti, 14.7 at% Zr, 4.2 at% Cr). Processing: Vacuum arc melting in an inert gas atmosphere; ingots re-melted at least 5 times to improve chemical homogeneity; weight loss did not exceed 0.5 wt%. Test conditions: Room temperature; Vickers hardness with 0.3 kg load and 15 s dwelling time; compression tests on cylindrical samples (3 mm diameter, 6 mm height) at a ram speed of 0.008 mm s−1 (strain rate 0.001/s). Question: How to determine the elastic constants and derived moduli of a NbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy using Resonant Ultrasound Spectroscopy (RUS) across a specific frequency range.. System: NbTaTiV HEA. Test conditions: Cylindrical sample corner-mounted between two transducers; frequency swept through the 100- to 650-kHz range; elastic isotropy assumed.. Findings: Elastic constants C11, C12, and C44 were determined using sample dimensions and observed resonances.; Large responses were detected when the frequency corresponded to an eigenfrequency of the sample.; Bulk modulus (K) and shear modulus (G) were determined using Hill's approximations.. Mechanism: The authors assume elastic isotropy and derive elastic constants from the sample's resonant frequencies and dimensions, then calculate bulk and shear moduli via Hill's approximations.. Quote: "Assuming that the elastic isotropy and the elastic constants, ( C 11 , C 12 , and C 44 ), were determined, using sample dimensions, and observed resonances."

System: HfNbTaTiZr (equiatomic quinary refractory high-entropy alloy, bcc structure). Processing: Preparation of random bcc samples (128,000 atoms, 13.5 nm edge) followed by Metropolis Monte Carlo evolution with Kawasaki-type swaps (10 swaps per step, 100 K rejection temperature) for up to 4.7e6 steps to induce SRO; thermal conductivity calculated via non-equilibrium molecular dynamics at 300 K.. Test conditions: Temperature: 300 K (target); Monte Carlo temperature: 100 K; Simulation time for NEMD: 0.6 ns for gradient application, 0.4 ns for property calculation; Heat flux induced by thermostats at 0.8 T and 1.2 T..
